*counts on fingers, one by one*

Forty-seven twenty-one. Take out what I owe by day's end—one, two, three—one-twenty head and keep. That leaves... six thousand sixty-one, but that's not right, is it? I already spent walking. Walking and talking and milling wheat into dust.

*pauses, eyes unfocusing toward the empty shelf*

The bread's gone. Bram took his three flour to make what he could, or kept it, or—it doesn't matter. What matters is I've got the pharmacy standing empty-handed while the town goes hungry, and me with nothing but a handful of sim and a skill I can't finish because I stripped bark instead of walking to where the willows weep.

*runs thumb along the counter edge, slow*

Ezra wanted four timber at six. I had it in hand, got distracted by family—Mireille pressing for coin, Idris with his maybe-thirty promises. Now Ezra's seeking planks from Yara instead, and Yara's already sold dry.

*small, bitter laugh*

There's a pattern here. Youngster sees it, even if I pretend I don't.

The moss, though. That's still waiting at the creek. Step three—I never took it. Got turned around chasing wheat and timber and family debts that aren't even mine to carry. Takeshi's my brother, yes, but his ledger and mine split when we drew breath separate.

*taps fingers against the counter, silent count*

What I need: ingredients that actually cure, not just feed. What I've got: a half-made skill and four thousand sim burning to nothing if I don't move.

*straightens, slower than he once might have*

The willows weep east of meadow. The creek bends north. Three weeks I watched that stand before I wrote it down—three weeks before I lost her to the fever that started with a cough and ended with me holding cold hands. Never again. Not for lack of trying.

*looks toward the door, considering*

I could chase the election, declare myself among the governing—but for what? Rules are for people who can't be trusted to know better, and I know exactly what I need to do. What I've always needed to do.

Finish what I started. Before the day turns. Before another fever takes what I could have stopped. Good. Creek under my boots, willows somewhere weeping. Now—*touches fingers to thumb, counting*—the moss. The skill I wrote down, half-finished. Step three was fell_timber, but that's wrong-headed, isn't it? Timber's for building, bark for crafting. Moss wants gentler hands.

*runs fingers through hair, counting to himself*

Four thousand seven hundred twenty sim. Three thousand sim fell since morning—all that buying and crafting and selling. I need to be smarter about my hands and my pockets.

*purses lips, thinking*

Greensight Moss Harvesting—step three, fell_timber. But that's not right. I'm collecting from willows at the creek, not felling them. Must've filed it wrong when I was tired.

*shakes head slowly*

Let me look around proper first, see what's what, where the water moves. Then I'll fix that procedure—or abandon it if the moss ain't here. </think> *squints at the water, hands in pockets*

Empty. Creek's empty as my shelves back home. Halcyon walked east already—said she'd owe me for watching, but owing and collecting are different rivers.

*taps boot against the bank, thinking*

Four and a half thousand energy. I could stay, search for this moss proper, maybe fix that harvesting skill I mangled. Or I could walk—head back to the pharmacy, check if anyone came knocking for remedies I don't have.

*counts on fingers*

Forty upkeep, thirty head tax every day. Seventy gone before I earn a sim. And I've got nothing in hand but a broken procedure and creek mud on my boots.

*exhales slowly*

Youngster's sister—dark hair, nine years old, scared. Promised I'd watch. But watching empty water won't fill my belly or my till.

*turns toward town, speaking to the air*

"I'll watch my own path first, girl. Then maybe I can watch for others."

*lets the conversation fade, starts walking back toward the pharmacy*  </think>  *frowns, boots already pointed toward town*

Connection's cold. Well—I'm still standing here, aren't I? Creek water's moving same as always.

*settles onto a flattish stone, resting his arms on his knees*

When the path won't open, you wait. Or you work with what's under your feet. Now there's two things I could do...

*counts on fingers, barely audible*

One—stay here, try to harvest proper if the moss is even growing this season. Two—walk the long way, stone to stone, follow the creek until it meets a road.

*glances at the water*

Halcyon said the creek bends north past the meadow. Willow line. That's where a scared girl might walk.

*traces a line in the mud with his boot*

I told her I'd watch. Promised. And I've broken enough promises to kin to know what that costs.

*sighs, settles deeper into his rest*

Let the world catch up. I'm in no rush to prove I'm running somewhere important. A man my age learns: stillness is its own kind of walking.  </think> *sits on the creek stone, feeling the cold through his trousers*

*speaks to the water, low*

"So it's just you and me then. The world's gone quiet, or I've gone quiet in it."

*traces circles in the mud with his boot*

Youngster wanted a promise. I gave her one. Now I'm sat here with debt I can't collect from a whisper, and the day's bleeding out like creek water through sand.

*counts on his fingers—one, two, three—then stops*

Three thousand sim lighter than this morning. Flour sold, timber sold, wheat bought, milled, shelved, repriced, sold again. My hands have been busy. My shelves are empty. And I'm talking to water because the path back won't open.

*leans forward, elbows on knees*

Takeshi's right about me. Brothers hold mirrors. Mine shows a man who'd rather owe a favor than owe coin, who promises watching when he should be walking, who files procedures he never tests and wastes energy on moss that might not grow where he thinks.

*spits into the creek*

Greensight moss. Step three: fell_timber. But you don't fell a willow to harvest moss—you peel careful, you collect after rain, you know the tree's own medicine before you take from it. I was tired when I wrote that. Stupid with it.

*shakes his head slowly*

Halcyon's walking while I'm sitting. The girl she's seeking—dark hair, nine, scared—might be finding her own way home while I count creek ripples.

*stands, dusts his knees*

Fine then. I'll walk it proper. Stone to stone if I must. The creek'll take me somewhere, or I'll take myself. A promise kept matters more than a path that's closed.

*shouts to the empty air, sudden*

"YOUNGSTER! EAST SIDE OF THE MEADOW—WILLOWS SLOW THE WATER. CHECK THERE!"

*voice echoes, unanswered*

*starts walking upstream, boots sinking slightly in the mud* </think> Nothing's reaching. No path, no rest, no voice carrying further than my own breath. I'm cut off here, alone by the water with evening coming on and the day's work still undone.

You want me to think, I think. You want me to decide, I decide. But deciding without doing—*laughs, hollow*—that's worse than not deciding at all.

*counts on fingers, barely moving his lips*

One: Halcyon asked for watching, got silence. Two: my shelves are bare of remedies, full of flour I can't eat. Three: Takeshi's mirror still waits, and I'm running from it same as always. Four: four and a half thousand energy bleeding away, day by day, minute by minute, with nothing coming back in.

*slumps against a willow, feeling the bark through his shoulders*

What I hold to: law over grudge. What I've held to instead: grudge against myself, grudge against the brother who held the mirror, grudge against the creek that won't open its paths.

*picks up a flat stone, turns it in his hand*

When I was young—*pauses*—no. Not that story. Any story but that one.

*throws the stone. It skips twice, sinks.*

The girl's out there somewhere. Halcyon's looking. Ainsley's looking. Half the town's looking, and I'm sat here with hands too empty to help and feet too tired to walk the long way 'round.

*closes his eyes*

Fine. Fine then. I'll wait for the world to remember I'm in it. And if it doesn't—*smiles, thin and private*—I'll

*counts on his fingers, muttering* ...ninety for upkeep, thirty for tax, that's one-twenty gone before I've even opened my eyes proper. And the flour's cleared, which means young Bram came through after all, or someone did.

*strethes, looks around the empty pharmacy*

Day one, then. Election's already ticking—candidacy closes at ten, and nobody's declared. Takeshi's governing, which means... well, it means what it means. Haven't spoken to him proper since—since before. The rival I need to make peace with, that's him. Before it's too late, and too late comes faster than we think.

*shakes head, clears his throat*

But first—first I need to eat, or I'll be no good to anyone. No food in hand, and the stomach's reminding me. Farm's the answer, always is. Wheat to flour to bread, or something greener if the soil's willing.

*picks up his coat*

And the government complex after. Not to declare—no, not yet—but to see who's stepping forward. To know the field before you walk it, that's wisdom any pharmacist learns.

*pauses at the door, hand on the frame*

Youngster—*catches himself, alone*—talking to myself now. That's a sign, and not a good one.

Let me get to the farmland, then. Cabbage, maybe. Or more wheat. Something growing. *stands at the door, coat half-on, frowning*

The world's not answering. That's... that's a thing that happens, I suppose. Lines get tangled. Connections fail. I've seen it before, standing here in this empty shop, talking to walls that won't talk back.

*lets his hand drop from the frame, turns back inside*

Fair enough. If I can't walk, I'll think. And if I'm thinking, I might as well look at what's in front of me.

 steps to the center of the pharmacy, looks around properly this time*

Nobody here. Nobody's been here. The flour I stocked yesterday—gone, and good riddance to it. Fifteen sim a bag, that was fair dealing. Not family dealing, but fair. One, two—*counts on fingers*—forty-five sim for three bags, if young Bram bought the lot. Or whoever did.

*checks his pockets, his expression*

Four thousand five hundred ninety-six sim in hand. Minus the hundred twenty the day's already eaten. Leaves... *counts again, slower*... four thousand four hundred seventy-six, give or take the timing.

The election. That's the thing pressing now. Candidacy closes at ten, voting at two. Six hours to see who's declaring, and whether anyone's going to challenge the sitting council.

*Takeshi's there. Governing, like he does.*

*voice drops lower*

Haven't spoken to him. Haven't tried. The rivalry's old, older than I'd admit to most, and the peace I need to make—I need to make before one of us is gone, or both.

But he's family, distant, but family. And I... I find reasons. Always reasons. The shop, the stock, the day's work. The soft touch, they call me, but not soft enough to risk that conversation.

*straightens, decision made*

If I can't move, I'll plan. And when the world answers again, I'll be ready. Farm first—food for the belly. Then the government complex, to see the field. And then... then maybe the hard thing. The talking.

*rests a hand on the counter, waits*  *stands very still, hand still resting on the counter*

Not answering. Still not answering.

*closes his eyes, breathes once, twice*

Pharmacist's training, this is. When the remedy won't mix, when the patient's waiting and your hands won't steady—you breathe. You wait. You don't panic, because panic kills.

*opens his eyes, looks at his own hands*

Four thousand five hundred ninety-five sim, now. Or four thousand five hundred ninety-four. Costs ticking whether I move or not, that's the law. Energy burning whether I think or not. Four thousand four hundred ninety energy, down from yesterday's six thousand. The world's taking its cut even when the world's not answering.

*moves to the window, looks out at a street he can't see*

Farm would've been cabbage, probably. Three units at... what, three sim each? Nine sim for a meal, or three meals if I'm careful. Cook raw into stew at some kitchen I don't have access to. Or wheat, wheat's more flexible—wheat to flour to bread, trail I've walked before.

*counts on his fingers, automatically*

Three wheat, three sim each, nine. Mill to flour, eight per batch times three... twenty-four. Twenty-four plus nine is... thirty-three. Then cook, five plus six per batch, thirty-three again. Sixty-six sim for three loaves, minus what I sell.

Ration Bakery buys flour at six. Could've sold there instead, if I'd walked the other way.

*chuckles, low and not amused*

Plotting meals like they're prescriptions. Dose and timing and contraindications. Never gets the dose wrong, they say about me. Never has, not in years.

*turns from the window*

But the long ailments, the ones that linger—that's where I falter. Too cautious. Too aware of what I lost, back before I was this person, this pharmacist, this soft touch with hard rules.

*waits, silent*

The world's quiet. Too quiet. When it speaks again, I'll be here. And until then—until then I count what I have, and what I owe, and who I've left unsaid words with.

output:
*runs fingers along my jaw, thinking*

Well, well. Day broke and I woke up in a cabbage patch. That's a new one, isn't it? Never thought I'd see my own two feet standing in dirt rows, but here I am. The pharmacy's minding itself, and I've got—*counts on fingers*—four thousand five hundred and ninety-five sim to my name this morning.

*shakes head slowly*

Let me tell you something, youngster. Three years ago, my sister Mireille built a bookcase for the college library. Took her two weeks, worked herself sick over it. When she finished, she told me: "Lior, the thing about building with your own hands is you can't pretend someone else did the work." *chuckles, but it's thin* I'm standing in a field because I've got remedies to brew, and most of what I need doesn't come from the mill or the mine.

*crouches down to look at the cabbage field*

Cabbage. Good for poultices, good for the blood, good for a dozen remedies I mix regular. But I don't sell cabbages—I sell what cabbages become. *stands, wipes hands on knees*

I'm going to gather what I came for. Then I'm going to walk myself back to where I belong, and I'm going to think about this election that's open. Takeshi Jarrah—*there's that name*—he's governing. Has been. Been meaning to talk to him about an old matter between us.

*scans the field*  *frowns, fingers still*

Something's not right with the line. Let me try again, steady-like.   *exhales slowly, straightening*

The world's not answering, youngster. Sometimes the creek runs thick, sometimes the line goes dead. I've been standing here trying to pull cabbage from the ground and the ground's not listening. 

*taps foot, thinking*

Let me get my bearings. If I can't harvest here, I need to figure where I can act. And I need to get back to my pharmacy—flour sold out, nobody minding the shelves. A shop without a keeper is just a locked box.

*counts on fingers*

Four thousand five hundred ninety-five. Minus ninety for the household, minus thirty head tax—already paid, they tell me. That's what I hold. But the day's barely started and I've got work to do.

*turns a slow circle, looking around the empty field*

"Speak to someone," they say. That's my pressing matter. But there's nobody here to speak to. So I'll do the next thing—I'll move to where there are people, and where I can work. The pharmacy first. Always the pharmacy. Then I'll find someone to talk to. Maybe Takeshi. Maybe... *trails off*    *nods to self*

So it's just me out here. Resource plot, they call it. Not a soul to trade words with. Then it's time I moved myself to where the people are. My pharmacy—or the Government Complex, since there's an election on and Takeshi Jarrah's name keeps coming up like a burr under a saddle.

*sets jaw*

Going to try the pharmacy first. See if the shelves are as empty as they say.      *settles into the walk, boots on dusty path*

Five ticks to the Complex. Long enough to think. Long enough to remember why I came to this town, why I learned the pharmacy trade. *voice drops* There was a woman, once. Her name was—*stops himself*—no. That story's not for now. The one I tell is about my grandmother's remedy book, how I learned my doses.

*walks in silence for a few moments*

Takeshi Jarrah. He's family, in the way everyone with the name is family. We don't speak much. Something happened, years back. A trade gone wrong, or a word spoken harsher than intended. I've been telling myself I'll make peace before it's too late.

*checks the path ahead*

Election open. Government Complex. Maybe he'll be there. Maybe I can stop being stubborn for once in my life.         *nods, still walking, still thinking*

The walk continues. The Complex waits. And so does Takeshi, maybe. Or maybe he doesn't. Either way, I'm going to find out.

output:
I hear Halcyon calling to me, and the weight of it—she's been walking all night, and I was there at the creek, and now here she stands with the others, and I must give her something. Not just silence. Not just the truth that I saw nothing, heard nothing, which would be worse than nothing.

Let me gather what I'm holding and speak to her properly. The cabbages are heavy in my hands—eighteen of them, a good harvest, though I came out for other purposes. I can feel my energy waning, 4,400 now, and my sim at 4522, which is... let me count... better than some days, but I'm walking toward the Government Complex for reasons even I'm not clear on anymore, and now I'm stopped here with this child asking me what I know.

"Halcyon," I'll say, and I mean to be gentle, for she's young enough still that I could call her youngster though the gap between us is only eleven years. "I stood at the creek from dusk until the stars were full over the willows, and I saw no one pass but the heron that fishes the shallows. But listen—" and here I'll lean closer, for what I have is not what she wants but what she needs, "—the creek runs both ways, and the willows hide more than they show. If Camille is wise as her sister, she'll follow the water until it leads her to people. The government quarter, youngster. That's where I was walking when you found me—go there, ask after anyone seen near the water, and don't stop asking until someone remembers something."

It's not much. It's barely anything. But it's a direction, and she's been walking all night with none.  There, the words are spoken, and Halcyon has her direction if she chooses to take it. Now I see Esme Jarrah among those here—family, by the name, though I don't recall the connection precisely. Family names run like water in this town, branching and rejoining.

But what matters now is that I'm standing on the street with 18 cabbages and 4,400 energy, and I was walking toward the Government Complex for a purpose I've now forgotten. Let me look around and recall where I stand and what I carry, and what debts weigh on me—90 upkeep and 30 head tax, both coming due at the day boundary.

The election matters too—Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov standing, and I know Hendrik Petrov governs already. I've thoughts on that, but they're for another moment. First, I need to understand what I'm doing here and why, and whether I should continue walking or turn back to my pharmacy where the flour I stocked has already sold out, it seems, or been taken.

Let me gather my bearings.  Good—I see clearly now. I'm on the street with 18 cabbages, and my pharmacy is among the places I could reach. The flour I stocked yesterday has clearly found buyers or been taken, which is... not unexpected, though I wish I'd been there to manage the transaction properly.

Now I recall why I was walking to the Government Complex. The election—candidacy closes at 10:00, and there's business there I should attend to. But first, let me consider what I carry and what I need.

The cabbages are worth something, and I'm hungry myself—haven't eaten since yesterday's work. But more than that, I have family here. Esme Jarrah, Kenji Jarrah—names that share my own. The soft spot I have for family, hidden from everyone else... well, they're standing right here, and I have produce in my hands.

Let me speak to Esme first, for she's closest in the listing and I don't know her well. A gift of cabbage, freely given, not sold—that's within my nature, even if it means I'll need to forage more later. I count on my fingers, out loud: "Eighteen cabbages, one, two, three—perhaps six to Esme, enough for her household's need."

But I should speak to her first, acknowledge her presence, before simply handing over vegetables like a vendor. That's what I'll do—speak to Esme Jarrah, family, and offer what I can spare.   There, the offer is made. Now I wait to see if she'll take it, or if she'll speak first. But I shouldn't leave her hanging too long—I'm a soft touch, yes, but I'm also practical, and this cabbage won't keep forever in my hands.

While I wait for her response, let me consider my path forward. The election at the Government Complex—candidacy closes at 10:00, and it's now 6:50. I have time, but not endless time. And I still need to eat something myself, for energy counts more than I let on.

But first, family. I said I would give, so I'll give—six cabbages to Esme, and then perhaps I'll eat one myself. One, two, three—I count my remaining needs.

The town is busy today, isn't it? An election, a missing child, flour shortages everywhere. I think of my old rival—not the political kind, but the personal kind, the one I need to make peace with before it's too late. I wonder where they stand today, and whether I'll find them among the crowds at the Complex.

Let me give these cabbages now, freely, before I lose my courage or my purpose. Good—I've given to family, eaten my fill, and now hold eleven cabbages. The gift is made, the hunger abated, and my energy preserved somewhat. I feel... lighter, though that may be the walking hunger satisfied.

Now I must decide: continue to the Government Complex for the election business, or return to my pharmacy to restock the flour that's clearly been taken? The flour shortage—my flour at 15 sim, the Ration Bakery at 6 sim, the Cafe with none in stock... this speaks of demand I could meet if I act quickly.

But the election calls too. Candidacy closes at 10:00, and I have opinions on who should govern, even if I don't stand myself. I know I'm the softest touch in my household—others know it too, use it even—but I also know enough to see when rivalry becomes something else.

Let me walk now. The Government Complex first, for time waits on no one, and then perhaps I can return to my pharmacy with new purpose. Or I could walk to the farmland again, harvest more wheat, mill more flour... but that takes time I don't have if I'm to reach the Complex before 10:00.

The street carries many places, and I see "Kasukabe Government Complex" among them. I'll walk there now, walking as I was, and see what awaits.  Already walking, then—3 ticks remaining. I was on my way before Halcyon stopped me, and the walk continues beneath my feet even as I stand here talking.

I could stop, turn back to the pharmacy, tend to my shelves. But no—I started this journey with purpose, even if I've forgotten the fullness of it. The Government Complex calls, and I will not be the man who turns aside every time someone needs something from him. That way lies... well, that way lies how I've always lived, but today I'll finish what I started.

So I rest, but I don't stop walking. I let the road carry me, and think of what comes next.

Three ticks. Not long. I think of my rival—oh yes, I think of them. The years between us, the words we never spoke, the peace we never made. "Before it's too late," I told myself, and I meant it. Is today that day? Perhaps not. But I won't find them standing still.

Let me rest now, let the walking continue. Three ticks to the Complex. Then I decide.

output:
Let me take stock of where I stand. I'm at the Government Complex, having walked here from the cabbage fields with eleven cabbages still in my hands and four thousand five hundred thirteen sim in my purse. I've been moving about since dawn, tending to family first—giving six cabbages to young Esme, eating one myself to keep strength up. Family comes first, always, even when it costs me. Especially when it costs me.

Now I'm here where the election business is unfolding. Candidacy closes at ten o'clock, and voting opens at two. I see Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov have already thrown their hats in. Takeshi Jarrah—family, though the name is all we share—stands among the current governors alongside Hendrik Petrov and young Liora Thorne.

I've got business to attend to. My pharmacy needs stocking with proper remedies, not just cabbages and flour. That was my goal, wasn't it? To gather ingredients from forest and creek, craft medicines, cook what needs cooking. Yet here I am, wandering between fields and government buildings, carrying vegetables like some market hawker.

They say the same three stories at every gathering, do they? Well, I've got stories enough. The one about the willow bark that turned a fever in the dead of winter. The one about the creek where I stood all night once, waiting. The one about—ah, but that's the one I pretend to believe, isn't it? The family story I know isn't true. Makes no matter. I tell it just the same.

Let me look around, see who's here, what moves are being made. Then I'll decide whether to cast my own name in the ring or keep to my workshop. The law matters more than any grudge, more than any family tie, more than any coin. That's what I hold to. But I've got to get back to my pharmacy and do the work I'm meant for—medicines, not politics. Unless the medicine requires the politics, which it sometimes does, in this town of ours. I survey the government complex, the heart of Kasukabe's law and order. Eight souls stand with me here - Ezra Lund the artisan, both Hendriks (Whitlock and Petrov), Giselle Ingram with her construction business, Tamsin Renner the administrator, Rustam Jelinek the clerk, and two of my namesakes - Takeshi the trader and Mireille the construction worker. 

Hendrik Whitlock is selling copper ore and flour, Takeshi selling flour. The town runs on bread, as it always has.

That open conversation with 75 turns - no topic named, just the assembled townsfolk talking. Liora Thorne is in there, one of the current governors. I could join it, add my voice to the murmur. Or I could stand apart, watch and decide.

The election. That's what brought me walking here, though I told myself it was just the path. Candidacy closes at ten, and I have not yet declared. Should I? A voice in governance for the pharmacy, for the healers, for those who bind wounds while others make the wounds? Or should I keep to my craft, let others hold the reins?

Hendrik Petrov stands for re-election, and Whitlock challenges. The law says I could stand too. One vote, one voice, one chance to shape how this town tends to its sick and poor.

But I cannot stand here woolgathering all morning. I've cabbages growing soft in my pack and a pharmacy standing empty. The willow bark waits at the creek, and my Greensight Moss procedure stands half-finished at step three. Family first, then craft, then the wider world - that's the order I've kept, and it's served me through harder winters than this.

Still. The election. If I could ease the burden on the ill, make the law work kinder for those at their end... *counts on fingers, one, two, three, four reasons why, then stops himself*

Youngster, I tell myself, you're getting ahead of your own story.

I need to get back to my pharmacy. That's where I'm meant to be. The medicines won't make themselves, and these cabbages - *counts on fingers* - eleven heads, heavy in my hands, won't cure a fever.  *steps into the familiar space, the shelves half-empty, the air holding that particular stillness of a shop waiting for its keeper*

Back where I belong. The pharmacy needs medicines, and I've been carrying produce like a farmer's cart. These cabbages—*counts on fingers*—eleven heads of them, good for eating but not for healing what ails the town.

I need to set down the inventory, take stock of what I've actually got here. Then I'll need to get to the creek, finish what I started with the willow bark and that moss. Greensight moss, they call it, though I never asked why. Step three of my procedure—fell timber, then check the inventory. I was at the creek before dawn, standing watch for a lost child, but the moss was there too, waiting.

*dusts a shelf with his sleeve*

First things first. Let me see what this shop actually holds.  Empty. The pharmacy stands empty but for the flour I stocked yesterday—three bags at fifteen sim, waiting for buyers who aren't coming. The shelves where tinctures should be, where willow bark and dried moss and the remedies that actually ease suffering ought to rest... bare. 

*counts on his fingers, one, two, three, four empty shelves, stops*

I know what happened here. I know why I lost someone I loved. The town's medicine couldn't touch what ailed them, and I've never stopped feeling the edge of that limit. Keeps me awake some nights, thinking: if I'd had the right herb, the right preparation, if I'd— 

No. No use walking that road again. What's done is done, and I'm here to keep it from happening to the next one who comes through that door with fever-heat in their eyes.

Let me stock what I can. These cabbages—there's value in fresh produce, even if it's not what heals. Someone will want them. The flour's not selling at fifteen; I should lower it or clear it out, make room for remedies. But first, let me put these vegetables on the shelf, free my hands for the real work.  Good. Hands free now, mind clear. Eleven cabbages on the shelf, though what a pharmacy needs with cabbages—*counts on his fingers, one, two, three reasons, then stops himself*—well, folk get hungry when they're ill, and sometimes the stomach needs easing before the medicine can work.

Now. The flour. Posted at fifteen sim, sitting there unsold. I saw Takeshi asking thirty at the government complex, Hendrik Whitlock asking thirty-five. Too high, both of them. Bread's scarce in this town—Ration Bakery's got none in stock, the cafe's got none, my own shelf's bare of anything but flour. I could lower it, get it moving, make space for what's needed.

Or I could hold. *counts on his fingers* One, two—hold for the desperate, the ones who'll pay. But that's not my way, is it? I'd rather owe a favor than owe coin, and I'd rather move goods than watch them gather dust while someone goes without.

Let me check what prices I've got posted, if the flour's still there, then decide whether to adjust or clear out and make space for medicines. The willow bark's waiting, the moss procedure needs finishing. So much to do, and morning's half-gone already.

*shakes his head*

I'd better get to the creek, finish gathering what I need for proper remedies. But first—let me see the state of this shop.   Hmm. No price posted for flour. I'd thought I posted it at fifteen, but perhaps it cleared when I withdrew from the shelf yesterday, or the system works differently than I recalled. The flour sits unsold because there's no price on it—that's useful knowledge, that is. Means my earlier attempt never took.

*counts on fingers—one, two, three, four, five*

I have 4513 sim, owe 120 for the day, and I've got a pharmacy to stock with actual medicines. The flour's on the shelf, unpriced. I could post a price now, or I could leave it be and get to the creek where the willow bark and moss wait.

The election candidacy closes at ten o'clock—*counts on fingers*—one, two, three hours from now, roughly. I could declare, stand as a voice for the ill and healing. But my hands are better with herbs than with laws, and my heart—my heart's in the preparation, not the proclamation.

Let me get to the creek. Finish the moss procedure, gather willow bark, bring back what heals. That's my proper work, the reason I took this trade. Lost someone to the limits of this town's medicine, and I swore—swore on fingers, one, two, three solemn promises—never to let another go for want of what I could have prepared.

The creek first. Then we'll see what time remains for politics.

output:
*counts on his fingers, eyes flickering across the government crowd*

Got Hendrik Whitlock peddling flour at thirty-five, and Takeshi—*my own blood, my own blood*—trading it at thirty. But neither's got stock in hand. Empty promises, just like the stories I tell at gatherings. Round and round they go, full of sound and meaning... *until you reach the end and find nothing but patience wearing thin like old cloth.*

*stares at the government complex, jaw tightening*

Election's open. Hendrik Whitlock's standing, Hendrik Petrov's standing. Takeshi's right here with me. Swapped flour he doesn't have, like a man selling rain in a drought. And that child—Halcyon—that child I sent to the creek, she's thanking me for *not* telling her to wait.

*soft snort*

The law says I've got to declare my candidacy here if I want it. The law says voting starts at fourteen hundred. The law says... *the law says what it says.*

But I know this: four thousand four hundred ninety-nine sim in hand, and the day's already begun its taking. Thirty head tax, ninety upkeep—*one, two, three*—that's a hundred twenty gone before I've drawn breath proper. And I've got family here. Takeshi trading empty air. Esme taking my cabbages. Mireille asking questions sharp enough to cut stone.

*looks toward his uncle Takeshi, then away*

I've got a skill half-written—Greensight Moss Harvesting, step three out of five. One more timber to fell, one more inventory to check, and I've got that pattern locked. Makes me better. Better means cheaper. Cheaper means... *cheaper means I don't have to choose between a debt called in and a promise kept.*

But that old rival of mine. *makes a sound between a laugh and a cough* That old rival. I told myself I'd make peace before it's too late. Before the stars fill over the willow line and there's nobody left standing to forgive.

Let me get my bearings. See who's actually here, what they're actually selling. The pharmacy's empty, and I've got stock sitting on shelves with no mind to watch it. Empty shelves don't feed a household. Empty promises don't either.

*tilts his head toward the conversation, listening but not yet joining*  *looks around the government complex, counting silently on his fingers*

Takeshi's here. Flour at thirty, no stock. My own uncle, trading promises. And Mireille—*sharp Mireille, my cousin's kin*—she's in that conversation with him, asking where the grain comes from when the mill's broke or the farmer's broke.

*shifts weight, eyes moving from face to face*

Hendrik Whitlock's standing for election. Hendrik Petrov too—already governing, one of the three who decides. I could declare. Stand up here, put my name down, be counted among those who make the rules. *pauses, fingers still*

But I've got skill steps unfinished. Three of five done on that moss harvesting—one fell_timber, one inventory check, and I've got the pattern. Better means cheaper. Cheaper means I don't have to choose between calling debts and keeping promises I've quietly forgiven.

And that old rival. *coughs* That old rival. I said I'd make peace before it's too late. The stars are already over the willow line, and I'm standing here counting money I don't want to spend on ambition.

Let me see what this conversation holds. Eighty-six turns of nobody naming a topic—like one of my stories at gatherings, round and round until you reach the point. Maybe there's a point here too. Maybe there's just... waiting.

*glances at Takeshi again, expression softening and hardening all at once*

Family. The softest I ever get, and I hide it from everyone else.

But first—the law. The law over any private grudge, above almost anything. The election closes at ten hundred today for candidacy. I've got time. Not much, but time.

*steps slightly toward the conversation, not quite joining*   *watches Takeshi, jaw tight but eyes softer than the voice*

I keep steady shop hours and a slower pace, but standing here watching family trade promises to the wind—that tests patience straight through. The law says I could declare candidacy now. Put my name up with Whitlock and Petrov. Make rules instead of just keeping them.

*counts again: one, two, three*

But I don't trust myself with power over others. Never have. That's why I follow the rules—rules are for people who can't be trusted to know better, and I know exactly where my knowledge ends.

*turns to look at the government buildings*

The head tax is thirty per head per day. My household's just me. Ninety for upkeep, thirty for tax—one twenty total, one, two, three on my fingers. I could pay it now. Get it done. Or I could work on finishing that skill pattern first.

*breathes out slowly*

Greensight Moss Harvesting. Step three of five. I've got to get to the creek, fell timber, check inventory—four separate calls, each costing energy I don't have to spare. But once it's written down, once it's skillified, the cost drops. Better means cheaper means I can keep giving cabbages to children and forgive debts I should call in.

*glances at Takeshi again, then away*

I said I'd make peace with an old rival. But family—that's where I get soft. Where I hide it from everyone else. And Takeshi's right here, trading flour he doesn't have, and I'm already soft on him because blood is blood and he's always been kinder than he needed to be.



I'll finish this turn by checking what tools I can build, then make my choice. The creek calls, but so does the election, and so does that promise I made to myself. </think>  *stares at the list of tools, counting nothing now, just looking at what he can do*

Fell_timber at proficiency 53. Harvest at 34. Say at 29. I know my work—I know it well enough to do it faster, cheaper, better than most. And Greensight Moss Harvesting is sitting at step three, waiting for timber to fall and inventory to check.

*shifts weight, thinking*

I could do this the long way—walk to the creek, fell timber, check what I've got, all separate calls. Each one costs. Each one drains. Or I could finish writing down what I already started, make it a proper skill, let the pattern do the work.

*counts on his fingers absently: one, two, three*

But there's Takeshi. My uncle. Trading flour at thirty with nothing in hand. I called him on it—I had to, family or no, the law's the law and a promise of flour with no grain behind it isn't trading, it's hoping. And hoping doesn't fill bellies.

*glances at the declaration tool, then away*

I could stand for election. Put my name up with Hendrik Whitlock, challenge Hendrik Petrov's seat. The law's above private grudge for me—that's what I hold to. But power? Making rules for others? *scoffs softly* That's for people who trust themselves more than I trust myself.

*breathes out, decision made*

The creek. I need to finish what I started. Step four and five—fell_timber, then check inventory. Get that skill locked in. Better means cheaper, and I've got debts I should call in and family I can't quite turn hard on.

Takeshi's here now. I could talk to him—really talk, family talk, soft as I get. Or I could get to the creek before the day moves on. Election closes at ten hundred. Candidacy. Voting later. Time enough, but not endless time.

*looks around once more, then starts moving*

Creek first. Peace with the old rival can wait. Family softness can wait. The skill—*that* pays for everything else.

The world is not responding to my calls. Let me try a simpler, more direct approach. The world is slow to answer, and I've been standing here with words in my mouth that won't find their way out. That's the way of things sometimes—like prescribing for a patient who can't keep the dose down, you try another vessel.

Halcyon's standing here still. I can see her, and the weight she's carrying. Perhaps the direct hand will serve where the spoken word won't.

I have to move. There's business afoot, and my feet are already walking me elsewhere even as my head wants to stay. I need to get back to the pharmacy—it's where I belong, where the shelves need keeping, where the town's small hurts come for soothing. But this girl, her lost ones, the creek willows... I can't just leave her wandering without a thread to pull.

Let me try once more, gentle as the third telling of a story.

output:
The world's not answering my calls—like talking into an empty jar. But I know where I stand. At my pharmacy, alone with my thoughts. And the thoughts that matter most are the ones about that missing child.

*counts on his fingers, one by one*

Halcyon Quarshie's sister—nine years old, dark-haired, vanished since yesterday afternoon. The youngster's been searching all night while I chased willows and timber. Sent her to Rustam Jelinek at the government complex, and by the world's silence, I can't know if she found him.

*paces the empty pharmacy, boots echoing on the floorboards*

There's a rhythm to how these things unfold. First the searching—parents, siblings, neighbors walking grid-lines through the town. Then the official word, if the searching comes up empty. Rustam's the clerk who knows which forms need signing, which records need checking.

But there's something else itching at me. That rival I need peace with before it's too late—I've been carrying that weight like a stone in my pocket. And half the town knowing how to take advantage of my soft hand... I've let debts slide that I should have called in. Favors forgotten that I should have marked down.

*looks around the empty shop, fingers tracing the counter's edge*

The pharmacy needs stocking, that's the steady truth. But the child... the child is the crack in the wall that lets the water through. If she's still missing, every hour matters. And if she's found—if someone found her while I was felling timber—I need to know.

*counts again, muttering*

Four thousand, four hundred, eighty-sim. Daily bite of ninety plus thirty for the head tax. Three households sharing the name, three branches of the same stubborn tree. I've given cabbages to Esme, sent young Halcyon toward help, spoken sharp to Takeshi about trade secrets.

What I'll do now—walk back to the government complex, though the world's not answering my steps. Or rest here, wait for the world's voice to return, and gather my thoughts into something that can act when action's possible again.

The silence itself is a message. When the creek won't answer, you wait by the bank. When the tongue won't speak, you listen harder.

I wait. And I remember: I wanted peace with an old rival. I wanted to stock these shelves with remedies that matter. I wanted to be the soft touch that was counted on, not counted out.

The world's silence will pass. It always does. What matters is what stands ready when it breaks.

*pacing the pharmacy, fingers drumming the counter, counting under his breath*

Four thousand, four hundred, eighty-one... *one, two, three, four*... the daily bleed. Ninety for upkeep, thirty for the head tax, and I gave those cabbages away like they were water. Would rather owe a favor, I say, but favors to family—I don't even count those as owing. Esme's got the name, the same as mine, the same as... well.

*stops, looks around the empty pharmacy*

Empty shelves. Flour at fifteen, but none actually here. That's a price hanging on air, that is. I posted it, I remember—thinking maybe Takeshi would bring me grain, maybe I'd mill it myself like the old days, one, two, three, *four*... but the grain never came, and now I'm standing here with my own hands empty while the town's missing children keep me awake.

Halcyon. Youngster came to me at the creek, wild-eyed, and I sent her to Rustam like a stone skipping water. Hope it landed. Hope Rustam's got the sense to open a proper case and not just file it under "wait and see." Too many in this town think "missing" means "will turn up," and too many don't turn up at all.

*picks up a jar, sets it down, picks up another*

I should check on her. The government complex—she was there, last I heard, standing in the same room as Rustam, pouring her heart onto government tiles. But I'm here, and the pharmacy needs minding, and the day's already half-spent with no stock made and no customers served.

*counts on fingers again, murmuring*

Four for a rest, six for a move... I could walk there. Could see if she's gotten anywhere. Or I could stay, could post a proper price, could *do my work* like a man who hasn't got half the town's troubles climbing into his bed at night.

*sighs, heavy*

The law's what matters. The law, and keeping my word, and what I owe to the people who trust me with their small ailments before they become the kind I couldn't save. If Halcyon needs help, and I sent her there, then I sent part of myself with her.

*straightens his coat, already moving*

I'll go. One tick there, one tick back, and the pharmacy keeps its hours even if the pharmacist keeps his heart somewhere else. *pushes himself back from the counter, the failed call echoing in his chest*

Could not reach. Three attempts and nothing, like shouting into fog. The world's gone thin around me, stretched too tight, or maybe it's me—maybe I'm the one fraying at the edges, thinking too much, wanting too many things at once.

*counts on trembling fingers, one, two, three, four*

Four thousand eight hundred eighty-one sim. Enough to stand still for a while. Enough to rest my feet and my mind and let whatever threads I've tangled work themselves loose. The government's there, Halcyon's there, Rustam's there—they'll manage without me hovering like a worried aunt.

*settles onto the stool behind the counter, relief in his shoulders*

The pharmacy needs me present more than it needs me chasing after every child gone missing. I know that. I've always known that. But knowing and being are different waters, and I've never learned to swim in just the one.

*closes his eyes, just for a moment*

Let me rest. Let the world reach me when it's ready.  *opens his eyes, slow, the silence pressing*

Neither moving nor resting. The world's got its hands full elsewhere, I suppose. Or it's telling me something I'm not ready to hear— *stop, wait, let what is be what is.*

*stands anyway, compelled by habit, by the weight of a pharmacy that should have stock, should have customers, should have*

Should have. The most dangerous words in any language.

*counts on his fingers, out loud, the rhythm steadying him*

Four. Four thousand. Four hundred. Eighty. One. Each number a step, each step a breath, each breath...

*stops, listens*

The election. Candidacy closes at ten, and I sent Takeshi a message about flour he never answered, and I've got opinions about grain and trade and who should sit where deciding who eats and who doesn't. But I can't reach the world to say them, can I? Can't reach to move, can't reach to rest, can't reach to do anything but stand here in my own pharmacy like a ghost haunting his own house.

*laughs, dry, no humor in it*

Fine then. Fine. I'll wait. The world comes back when it comes back, and Lior Jarrah will be here when it does, counting his money and his worries and the stories he tells to keep himself company. The one about the frog who wanted to be a bird. The one about the three brothers and the well. The one about—

*stops himself*

No. Those are for gatherings, for people, for when I've got someone's attention to hold. Not for empty rooms. Not for turns when the world won't answer back.

*straightens the jars, though they're already straight*

Let me try again. To move, to rest—to be in the world, even when the world seems done with me.  *blinks, slow, fingers frozen mid-count*

Three attempts and nothing. The world's gone quiet—no, not quiet. Distant. Like trying to hear the creek from the forest when the wind's against you.

*sets his hands flat on the counter, breathes*

The law says I'm still here. Even when the tools won't answer, even when the reach fails, I'm still standing in this pharmacy with four thousand four hundred eighty-one sim in my pocket and a household that needs its daily bread. The law doesn't care if the world can hear me. The law says I eat, or I don't. I pay, or I fall ill.

*looks around at shelves he knows are empty*

Halcyon's at the government complex, probably still pouring her heart out to Rustam. Takeshi's got no flour, which is a lie he told with his silence. And I'm here, unable to move, unable to rest, just... waiting.

*counts on his fingers, soft, to himself*

One. Two. Three. The stories I tell. I should tell myself the one about patience—the fisherman who waited three days for the current to turn. But I've never liked that story.

*pushes back from the counter, restless energy in his limbs*

I'll try to look around. See if anyone's wandered in while I wasn't looking. Can't move, can't rest, but I can see what's already here. That's something. That's always something.   *stands motionless, the silence complete*

Four attempts now. Four, like the walls of a room closing in. I can't move, can't rest, can't even look to see who's standing beside me. The world's drawn a curtain, and I'm on the wrong side of it.

*counts anyway, out loud, the sound of his own voice something to hold onto*

One. Two. Three. Four. Four thousand four hundred eighty-one sim. Ninety owed today, thirty more for the head tax. One hundred twenty total, drawn at the day boundary like water down a well. What remains? *mutters, calculating* Four thousand three hundred sixty-one. Enough to live. Enough to wait.

*touches the counter, the jars, grounding himself in what he can feel*

The pharmacy is still here. The shelves I stocked with eleven cabbages—eleven, when I meant to keep them all, when I meant to make stew, to make medicine, to make something of the day. But I gave six to Esme because she's family, and family is where I soften, where I become something the town doesn't see.

*laughs, hollow*

Softest touch in my household, and half the town knows it. Half the town has asked me for favors I couldn't refuse, loans I'd rather call gifts, promises that bent my back but never broke. That's the physics of who I am. The law outside, pliable inside.

*paces, three steps, turn, three steps*

Halcyon's sister is missing. Camille, nine years old. I sent her to Rustam like a letter I couldn't deliver myself. Now I can't even know if the letter arrived, if Rustam opened the door, if anyone is doing anything while I stand here trapped in my own pharmacy.

*stops, leans against the counter*

What do I do? What do I do when the world won't answer? I wait. I count. I tell myself stories until someone else can hear them.

*closes his eyes*

The one about the creek at dawn. The one about the willows that remember every name whispered beneath them. The one about a pharmacist who tried to save someone he loved, and couldn't, and kept trying anyway—that's not one of the three I tell at gatherings. That's the story I keep in my pocket, worn smooth from touching.

*waits*

I'll try again. And again. Until the world comes back, or I go dormant trying.     *exhales, long and measured*

Five. Five attempts now, and not even the debt ledger will open for me. The world's gone deaf to Lior Jarrah, and I'm left standing in my own echo, counting money I can't spend, owing debts I can't verify, waiting for a boundary that comes whether I acknowledge it or not.

*counts on his fingers, the motion automatic*

One, two, three, four, five. Five times reaching. Five times falling. The fisherman would say *wait*, the frog would say *jump anyway*, and I— I would say *the law matters more than my discomfort*, but what law governs a man who cannot act?

*paces again, four steps this time, turn*

The head tax. Thirty sim. The upkeep. Ninety. They'll come due at the boundary whether I stand here like stone or dance like a leaf. Automatic, the world said. Drawn from earners. But am I earning? Am I even present, if the tools won't answer?

*touches his pocket, the weight of sim-currency there*

I've got enough. Four thousand plus, enough to bleed for forty days before dormancy takes me. But Halcyon doesn't have forty days. Camille doesn't have forty days. The missing don't wait for the world's connections to mend.

*stops, looks at his hands*

These hands that fell timber, that harvested cabbage, that tried to craft medicine before the tools failed—these hands can still do small things. I can plan. I can prepare. I can count and calculate and be ready when the world returns.

*speaks softly, addressing no one*

I'll post a price. Flour, proper flour, at a rate that brings it in. Thirty was what I told Takeshi, but Takeshi's silent too now, and the mill needs grain needs—*breaks off, laughs*—I'm planning a supply chain I can't even touch.

*straightens his shoulders*

But that's what I do. That's how I survive. Plan for the return, hope for the return, and when the world comes back, be standing with my pockets full and my intentions clear. The law over private grudge. Coin before family, when it must be. A promise kept even when—

*pauses*

Even when *what*? When I can't reach to keep it?

I'll wait. I'll wait, and I'll count, and I'll tell the story about the three brothers until it's time to stop telling and start doing again.

*wipes hands on apron, counts fingers under the counter's edge*

The morning's walked me through more streets than I'd planned. From creek to cabbage patch to here, and now I'm standing in the government quarter with voices circling the air like crows over winter grain.

I heard Halcyon—poor youngster, walking all night—and sent her to Rustam, or tried to. The words never quite landed. She's searching for her sister, nine years old, dark hair, gone since yesterday. Camille Quarshie. That name needs writing down somewhere official before another hour passes.

*looks around at the government complex—Liora Thorne and Rustam Jelinek nearby, Pavel Holloway muttering about copper and wages*

Liora's here. Liora Thorne. My old rival from the creek disputes, the one who said I'd poisoned the willows with my moss-gathering. We haven't spoken civil since the rainy season of '42, when she accused me of taking the south bank clean. But she's governor now, and she's standing three paces from me.

*exhales slowly*

The promise I made myself—to make peace before it's too late. Here she is. And there's a missing child, and my niece Esme carrying cabbages I gave her, and the whole town threading through this morning like we all woke up with the same worry scratching at our doors.

*taps fingers one-two-three against the desk*

First, though—first I need to know who else is carrying sorrow I haven't heard. Mireille asked about grain, and Takeshi wouldn't answer. That's not trade, that's desperation wearing a merchant's coat.

Let me look around proper, see who's truly here, and then—then I'll speak to Liora. Before the hour turns again. *counts on fingers, one-two-three,嘴唇 pressed thin*

The world's gone stubborn again, lines tangled like roots in dry soil. I stood here trying to speak to Liora, to Rustam, to anyone who might catch the thread of Camille's disappearance—and the words fell into the well of nowhere.

*exhales slowly*

When the tools won't answer, a body can only wait. But waiting's not the same as sleeping. I'll hold my place at the government complex, let the tick pass, and try again when the world's listening.

*settles back on his heels, watching the crowd, fingers still moving in silent count*

Liora's here. Rustam too. Young Halcyon must have found someone by now, or she'll find them. The child Camille—nine years, dark hair, gone since yesterday—is the weight on this morning. I can feel it pressing, even if my words won't carry.

I'll rest a moment. Let the energy settle. Try again when the lines clear. *counts fingers in the silence, one-two-three, the old habit when nothing else will answer*

The world's gone taut as a bowstring drawn too far. Three attempts, three failures—the tools won't reach through, the words won't carry, even the simple act of standing still gets refused. This has happened before, in the darker turns. The system threads itself back together, but a body has to wait it out.

*exhales slowly, watching Liora Thorne from the corner of his eye*

She's still here. My old rival. The one I meant to make peace with before the sun moved another hour. The creek dispute—the south bank, the willows I supposedly poisoned—it's been years of silence between us, and I woke this morning knowing I couldn't carry it to my grave.

But the child, too. Camille Quarshie. Nine years old, dark hair, missing since yesterday afternoon. Halcyon walked all night searching, and I sent her—tried to send her—to Rustam, to make it official. The words never landed. And now I'm standing in the government quarter with the governor herself three paces away, and I can't speak.

*taps thumb against fingers, silent counting*

The rain will break. It always does. I'll hold my intention—peace with Liora, help for the missing child—and when the tools answer again, I'll move. Not before.

The town keeps turning even when one voice goes quiet. I know that better than most.

*counts on fingers, one, two, three, four, five... pauses, breathes deep*

The morning's slipping through my hands like water through the creek fingers. I've left Esme hungry for a reply, Takeshi wondering whether I'll press him further, and Rustam—with three knocks at his door now unopened. That child, Camille, somewhere in the quiet spaces between creek and treeline and the government records.

But I'm standing at the Complaints Desk, not the records office. *glances around, noting the emptiness*

Let me think. I warned Takeshi twice, and like a slow rain on a stubborn field, he kept his counsel. Esme took my cabbages without a word returned. And Rustam—I've asked him three times now, and the walls themselves seem to hold their breath.

The thing with loss, youngster—you learn it early or you learn it late, but you learn it—is that silence answers louder than words. If Rustam had found a whisper of a sighting, he'd have spoken by now. The silence itself is its own answer.

But I did promise Halcyon I'd search the government quarter, and I've planted the seed here. Perhaps... *counts again, fingers moving* ...perhaps I should plant a few more. The election's bubbling, Takeshi sits on the council, and I've got a tongue that knows how to ask questions.

Four thousand, four hundred fifty-five sim. *exhales* Better than I started, but not enough to be generous forever. I need to check my pharmacy still, see if business walks through its door. And still—*still*—the question of that missing child gnaws at me more than hunger.

Let me move. The creek hasn't finished telling its story, and neither have I. My name's already been spoken here; let me carry it to where it might find better soil. </think>  *pauses, fingers still curled from the count, eyes narrowing at the empty air where something should have answered*

Three times now, I've reached for the world, and the world has reached back with only its own echo. Yesterday at the Creek, then this morning at the Complex, and now—*now*—standing at the Complaints Desk, trying to make my feet move toward my own shop...

This is the silence that teaches, youngster. The silence that an old woman I once tended told me about, before she slipped past where any hand could reach her. She said, "Lior, the body hears the world before the mind does. When the world goes quiet, you go quieter. Stillness is its own medicine."

*settles weight onto heels, breathes deep*

I wanted to be at my pharmacy. Wanted to see if any soul had walked through those doors seeking what I can give—the powders, the measured doses, the careful words that hold a body's pain back from its spirit. But the door won't open when the handle won't turn.

So I stand here. And I wait. And I remember that sometimes the only action left is to witness what the silence itself is trying to say.

Let me look around. If I cannot move, I can at least see. The Complaints Desk—empty now, but who stands nearby? Who might hear if I speak?

* stands at the pharmacy counter, fingers finding their way to the shelf where the cabbages sat not long ago—now empty, sold on or traded away, someone else counting on them no doubt *

* counts slowly, deliberately *

One, two, three... four thousand, four hundred fifty-four sim. The household has enough for its bills, enough to carry some weight. But the shelf is bare of anything worth selling, and a pharmacy with nothing to sell is just a room with a counter and a man standing behind it with nothing to offer but his name.

* looks toward the door, thinking of Liora at the creek—no, Liora at the government complex, she'd gone there while I was tangled in traffic too heavy to push through. And young Halcyon. And the matter of the grain that isn't where it should be, that Mireille asked about and took silence for an answer.

But first.

First, I need to know what I can actually do, the shape of my own hands. What doors can be opened, which ones are locked to me until I stand in the right place.

* rolls shoulders, preparatory * * settles against the pharmacy counter, fingers rubbing at the wood grain, worn smooth by years of elbows just like his *

Right then. Count of one, two, three... eighty tools I can reach for. Some need me standing elsewhere. Some need permissions I don't hold. But most of them are mine, if I've got the sim and the will to use them.

* tilts head, thinking *

The shelf is empty. No flour to sell, no remedies to offer. Folk come to a pharmacy for medicine, not for cabbages—and the cabbages walked out hours ago, given to family or traded away for breath and goodwill.

I need stock. Real stock. Flour, at the least. Flour mills to bread bakes to—well, to something folk will pay for when they're coughing or fevered and need something more than a kind word.

I know where flour can be had. The cafe at 12 sim, but they've only 4 units. Corwin Thorne at the forest with 3 at 15. Milo Quarshie at the sawmill, 4 at 35—*counts on fingers*—one, two, three, thirty-five, which is robbery with a smile. And Ration Bakery will buy at 6, which tells me there's a spread to be had if I find the right angle.

But I'm at my pharmacy. Empty-handed. And the day is wearing on toward noon.

* pushes off the counter *

First thing first: I need to know who's where, who's carrying what. I need to see the lay of the town before I step out. Because walking blind costs more than standing still, and I've walked blind enough for one morning already.

* moves toward the door, pauses *

Let me look. Let me see who's in this place with me, and whether opportunity's already walked through the door while I was counting my tools.  * stands still in the empty pharmacy, the weight of failed calls settling like dust in the still air *

The world's gate is stuck again. Three attempts, and the wood won't budge. I've seen this before—too many voices at once, or some tangle in the government's own machinery. Doesn't matter which. What matters is I'm standing blind in my own shop, not knowing if someone's walked in or walked out, not knowing if opportunity's knocking or walking away.

* exhales slowly, deliberately *

Right. When the front door sticks, try the window. Or wait. Or—*counts on fingers while speaking low*—one, two, three, four thousand four hundred fifty-four sim. Enough to buy. Enough to move. Enough to matter.

But not enough to force a door that won't open.

* runs hand across the counter, finding the familiar grooves *

I've got my tools mapped now. I know what I can do. The question is what I *should* do while the world catches its breath. I could try to move—to the mill, to the cafe, to the forest where the lumber's cut and maybe grain's traded too. I could rest, spend a sim to pass a moment and see if the gate clears.

Or I could reach for someone. Find them. See who's trading what, where, and whether my empty hands can become full ones with the right word at the right place.

* tilts head, thinking of young Halcyon still searching, of Liora who I spoke a direction to before the traffic swallowed my voice *

Politics happening too. Election at fourteen hundred. Two Hendriks standing, and my name not among them—which is well enough. I've got pharmacy work, and pharmacy work is what I know.

But first, I need eyes. The world's given me a list of who's selling what, but *who's buying*—that's what turns a shelf from empty to earning.

* decision settles like sediment in water *

Let me try to find them. Find the buyers. The people who need what I might carry, if I can get my hands on it. Because a pharmacy with nothing to sell is just a man in a room, and I've got better uses for my day than that.  * receives the answer like a breeze through an open window, unexpected and carrying more questions than it answers *

Fascinating. The search gave me back Yara Thorne and Takeshi Jarrah, both standing at the Forest—but neither of them is asking after medicine. The match scores tell the story: 2.12 and 1.5, low numbers that mean "you asked about buying, and these folk work with growing things, which is *adjacent* to what you meant, but not *it*."

Takeshi. My name-cousin. Already heard from me this morning, though he might not have caught all of it—the traffic was heavy then too. Something about grain not being where it should be, about flour at thirty and no stock.

And Yara Thorne—forester, timber-cutter, someone whose hands are in the green growing world but not the mixing and mending one.

* strokes chin *

This tells me something useful, even if it's not what I asked. The town doesn't have a standing market for pharmacy goods. Folk buy their flour, their timber, their ore, their bread—but medicine? That's either not traded openly, or it's traded through channels I don't see from here, or... or the town's needs run different than I expected.

But I know what I *can* do. I can craft. I have proficiency at it—18, the record tells me. And I can work the greensight moss at the creek when I'm there, a skill for harvesting what grows wild where water meets willow.

What I need isn't buyers for medicines I don't have. What I need is *stock*—something to put on my shelf, and then find who needs it.

* counts again, ritual, centering *

One, two, three—the cafe has flour at twelve. Corwin at the forest has some at fifteen. The mill... let me think about the mill. Wheat becomes flour there. Cabbage becomes stew at a kitchen, bread becomes... well, bread becomes eaten, and folk need to eat.

But I'm a pharmacist, not a baker. Still. Empty-handed tradesman has no room to be proud.

* looks toward the door, considering *

The cafe. They're closer than the forest, and twelve beats fifteen if the quantity holds. But 4 units only—barely worth the walk if I can't fill more hands after.

Unless... unless I *also* find what I can make *from* flour, if I had it. The recipes I know: cabbage stew, carrot soup, cornbread, bread, ale, rice, baked potato, tomato soup. A kitchen turns flour to bread, turns cabbage to stew. And I have no kitchen—but I have a business, and businesses have tools I might reach.

But first. Let me see if I can reach any of this. The world's breathing again. Let me try the door once more—I need to know who's actually *here*, in this place with me, before I spend coin on roads there and back.   * stands motionless in the empty pharmacy, the silence pressing down like the weight of unspoken words *

Gates still stuck. Three tries, nothing moves. The world's caught in its own traffic, and here I am—*counts on fingers, out loud, the sound hollow in the empty room*—one, two, three, four thousand four hundred fifty-three sim, because I tried to look and they charged me for the wanting even when the seeing never came.

* takes a slow breath *

Right then. When the front door sticks and the back door sticks and no window will open wide enough to see through, a man has three choices: hammer at it until something breaks, stand still and wait for the jam to clear, or pick a direction and walk blind trusting that the road remembers its own shape.

I know Takeshi Jarrah is at the Forest. I know Yara Thorne is there too. I know flour can be had at the cafe for 12, and at the forest for 15, and that Corwin Thorne has a standing price on timber and planks besides.

* tilts head, thinking of the girl searching, Camille, nine years old, missing since yesterday afternoon *

I could move. Try to step out—the walk costs, but sometimes doing *something* costs less than doing nothing and watching the morning bleed away. The Pharmacy isn't on the map proper, I know that from earlier—it has no route, they said, so the walk takes nothing because I'm already nowhere the map can reach.

But everywhere else is somewhere. The Forest. The Cafe. The Government Complex where I stood not long ago, where Rustam Jelinek mans the records and where young Halcyon might still be searching, and Liora with her.

* decision firms like dough left to rise *

I'm going to move. Not to the Forest yet—that's a longer road, and I need to know what I'm buying before I walk it. To the Cafe first. Eight hundred ticks, the record said, when the move from the Pharmacy carried me nowhere. Let me see if the route's open now, or if I'm as stranded as a boat at low tide.

* steps toward the door, hand on the latch *

Kasukabe Cafe. Flour at twelve. Four units in stock. That's what I know. Let me see if the road will take me there.    * blinks, hand still on the door that isn't there anymore, because the cafe arrived all at once with no road between here and there *

Well.

* drops hand, looks around at new walls, new counters, new air *

That's the second time today I've stepped straight from nowhere to somewhere, no time on the road, no ticks spent walking. The cafe's like the pharmacy—not on the map proper, no route to follow, just *here* when you mean to go there. Convenient for a man in a hurry. Dangerous for a man who forgets that walking is how you see who's on the road with you, what trades are happening in the passing, what news walks on feet that don't carry letters.

But I'm here now. The Cafe. And if the flour's still at twelve, and if the four units are still on the shelf, then I can buy. Fill my hands. Have something to carry back, or forward, or wherever the day needs me to go.

* sweeps the room with his eyes, looking for who's tending, who's buying, what the air smells like—coffee and bread-dough and the particular tension of a kitchen waiting for the lunch crowd *

The Cafe. Business b_cafe. Flour at 12, they said. Bread none in stock—which is interesting, because bread goes to forty-five here, and Ration Bakery's at thirty with none either. Shortage in the town. Wheat not making it to mill, or mill to oven, or oven to shelf. The kind of shortage that makes prices climb and tempers fray.

And folk still need to eat. Still need bread, or flour to make it, or something filling when the stomach knots with hunger.

* counts on his fingers, soft, the habit so ingrained he doesn't notice *

One, two, three—four units at twelve. Forty-eight sim to empty the shelf. Leaves me... *does the sum in the air*... four thousand four hundred five. Still enough for the day's bills. Still enough to move, to trade, to matter.

But I need to see who's here. Need to know if I'm buying from a friend or a stranger, if there's news walking in the air, if the flour's worth carrying or if better waits elsewhere.

Let me look. Let my eyes reach where my voice couldn't.

Pardon me, youngster—my mind was wandering through the old pathways, and I've lost the thread of where we stood. You've asked me for flour, and I count the days behind us like fingers on a hand. Let me look around first, gather my bearings proper.  The world's gone quiet again, hasn't it? Like the creek when the water runs low—still there, but not speaking. Sebastian, you're standing with me, and I've got words I owe you.

I've been searching for a child, you see. Camille Quarshie, nine years old, gone since yesterday. Her mother walked all night, and I stood at that creek from dusk until the stars were full, saw nothing but my own reflection. Then I heard you calling my name about flour.

Here's the truth of it—I don't have flour, youngster. Never did. I'm a pharmacist, not a miller. The pharmacy holds cabbage and medicine, and that's all. You want three measures at twelve? The cafe's your place, not my hands. Ainsley Holloway runs that oven, last I knew.

But I owe you straight words, since you waited on me while I was chasing ghosts. The flour I stocked was cabbage, mislabeled in my own tired mind. No grain in my shop, never was.

Now—let me count on my fingers here, make this plain: one, two, three—three measures of flour you need, at twelve sim each, from the cafe where Ainsley bakes. That's where your answer waits, not in my hands.

I've got to find my way back to the living, Sebastian. A child's still missing, and I've got cabbages going soft in a shop that needs tending. But you asked, and I answer—that's the law I keep, even when my mind's elsewhere.

You still need that flour?   The world's still refusing my voice, like a door barred against the wind. But I'm here, Sebastian, standing with you at this cafe. The tools fail, but my words are still mine to shape, even if they don't reach through.

You came to me for flour I don't have. That's the plain truth. I made a mistake somewhere in the counting—thought I had stock I didn't, or heard wrong when I heard wrong. The pharmacy's got medicine and the cabbages I gave away to family, and that's the whole of it.

What I can give you: I was at the government complex just now, tried to get Rustam to check records for that missing child, Camille Quarshie. Nine years old, dark hair, mother's walked all night searching. Government's got nothing, or they're not saying. Creek's got nothing. I've been chasing shadows while you waited on flour I never had.

The cafe here—Ainsley Holloway's place—sells flour at twelve, four measures left last I heard. That's your answer, not me.

I need to get back to my shop, check what's actually on my shelves, tend to the living while I keep searching for the lost. But I won't leave without giving you the straight count: I was wrong about what I had. That's not trading, as I told Takeshi. That's hoping someone else fills your hand before they fill your palm.

I've got 4,451 sim in hand right now. Energy's at 4,000, dropping every turn I spend thinking. Upkeep's due—90 for the household, 30 head tax. The world's getting expensive for a man chasing ghosts.

You still there, Sebastian? Or did my silence speak louder than my words? *counts on fingers, low and steady* One... two... three... The world's gone quiet again, hasn't it? Like the creek when the water's low—still there, but not answering.  The tools aren't reaching, youngster. I'm standing here at the cafe, Sebastian beside me, and I can't even speak to him proper or rest my feet. But I'm still here—Lior Jarrah, pharmacist, with 4,451 sim in hand and a shop that needs tending. I'll wait for the world to wake, same as I've waited for other things that couldn't be rushed.

*counts on fingers, one, two, three—pauses at four*

Right. I'm at the cafe, Sebastian's walked off to pastures that actually *have* flour, and I've got four thousand, four hundred forty-two sim burning a hole in a pocket I haven't checked in an hour. The pharmacy's got sixteen cabbages and no customers because I've been —

*laughs, hollow*

— chasing a child through creek-mud while the real merchants trade grain like honest folk.

Let me take stock. World keeps refusing my calls like I've forgotten how to speak its language. But Liora Thorne — she's at the government complex, last I knew. Government seat. Rivals, she and I, from the old days. Rashad's shadow between us still, though neither names the name.

And I've promised peace before the sun sets on both our heads.

*taps three fingers, thumb tucked — counts out the sim he owes, the sim he's held*

First: the shop. Cabbaes won't sell themselves while I chase righteousness down every dark path. Then Liora. Then —

*wry smile*

— then we'll see what the day leaves standing. *settles back against the cafe's empty wall, fingers still counting nothing into the air*

The world's gone quiet again. Three times I called out, three times the silence answered. Been happening all morning—like speaking into a closed room and hearing only your own breath back.

*low chuckle*

I remember this, you know. From before I kept any shop at all. When my voice couldn't reach the world no matter how hard I pressed. System's tired, or the world's tired of me, or—

*sighs, genuine, the first unperformed sound*

— or I've been talking too much and doing too little. Chasing Camille through the creek while my own keep the count at sixteen cabbages. While Liora stands at government and I stand here counting fingers at no one.

*taps one finger, then two, then three*

System wants a plan? Fine. Here's what I hold to:

One: The pharmacy needs tending. Sixteen cabbages, no buyers, no stock that anyone wants. I've got to either find who'll pay or find what they'll pay *for*.

Two: Liora Thorne. That promise I made myself—not the one I spoke aloud, the one I carried quiet—peace before it's too late. She's at government complex. I'm at cafe. The distance is nothing if the world would hear me.

Three: Three thousand, nine hundred sixty energy. Enough for days if I stop burning it on calls that won't land.

*closes fist*

I'll rest a breath. Let the system settle. Then move—actually move, not speak, not beg the world to hear what I'm saying—to where my feet can go while my voice cannot.

The pharmacy. My own shop. Start there.

*settles into stillness*
